Business goal: Allow features to record asynchronous work intent durably as part of the same domain transaction that creates the business state requiring that work.
User outcome: Feature workflows can request background work without risking a committed domain record with a missing queue request.
Notes / constraints: This is the transactional outbox-facing enqueue seam. It should accept small versioned JSON payloads stable entity references execution scope queue defaults priority retry policy selection and idempotency key. It writes durable outbox/job metadata in PostgreSQL and does not require the caller feature to import BullMQ Redis or provider-specific types.
Tenant context rule: tenant-scoped callers must pass exactly one tenant context when the job type is tenant scoped; root and platform-internal jobs must declare their scope explicitly
Allowed root roles: RootUserAdmin for future manual/operator enqueue if exposed later
Explicitly denied roles: unauthenticated callers; tenant actors unless a tenant feature explicitly exposes an approved capability
Authorization summary: Normal feature code may enqueue through the internal seam after its own capability has authorized the business action. No public enqueue API exists in v1.
Backend enforcement rule: The service must validate registered job type scope payload version idempotency key and payload-safety rules before persisting a durable request. It must not publish directly to BullMQ when enqueueing participates in a domain transaction.
Session / expiry behavior: No browser session behavior in v1. Request actor may be stored only as audit attribution not as replay authority.
Request contract: Input includes jobType queueName or default selector payloadVersion payload idempotencyKey optional runAt priority executionScope tenantId when required requestedBy audit attribution and retry policy override constrained by job-type policy.
Response contract: Returns durable job request metadata including jobId status queuedAt effective queue priority payloadVersion and idempotency result.
Error contract: Validation error unknown job type unsupported payload version unsafe payload forbidden secret-bearing field missing tenant context for tenant job duplicate idempotency key and persistence failure.
Cross-feature seams: Future consumers include notificationDelivery tenantAuth tenantAdmins imports exports campaigns and maintenance workflows.
Persistence impact: Creates durable job and job-outbox records plus idempotency metadata. Does not create BullMQ jobs directly when inside a durable domain transaction.
Indexes / uniqueness: Unique active idempotency key per job type where supplied. Index on status queueName jobType runAt priority createdAt and dispatch state.
Search / filter model: Filtering deferred to future operator APIs. Internal repository must support dispatcher polling by undispatched status runAt and priority.
Session / auth dependency: No direct session dependency for internal seam. Calling feature owns request authn/authz before enqueue.
Compatibility / migration notes: Provider boundary must allow BullMQ Redis first while preserving future SQS or RabbitMQ adapter replacement. Payload contract must stay provider-neutral.
Authentication requirement: No external authentication at this seam.
Authorization enforcement layer: Feature service boundary plus job registry validation. Calling feature enforces user-facing authz.
Audit requirement: Audit attribution should be persisted when supplied and operator/manual enqueue must be audited if added later.
Privacy / personal data impact: Payloads may contain personal-data references but should not contain secrets tokens credentials or broad permission claims. Full payload display must be redacted in future operator views.
Standards impact: High reliability anti-drift and security relevance because this seam connects domain transactions to asynchronous execution.
Acceptance notes: Acceptable when a feature can atomically persist business state and a durable job request without depending on BullMQ APIs or losing enqueue intent on process crash.

Business goal: Publish durable undispatched job requests to BullMQ after the owning database transaction commits.
User outcome: Committed feature work eventually reaches the Redis-backed queue even if the original web process crashes after commit.
Notes / constraints: A dispatcher process reads durable outbox rows and publishes provider-neutral requests to BullMQ. Once BullMQ accepts the job the outbox row is marked dispatched with provider metadata. Dispatch should be idempotent and safe to retry.
Tenant context rule: no tenant decision is made by the dispatcher; tenant context remains payload/context metadata validated by the registered handler
Allowed root roles: RootUserAdmin for future manual dispatcher controls if exposed
Explicitly denied roles: unauthenticated callers; normal tenant actors; direct client dispatch calls
Authorization summary: Only internal platform worker runtime dispatches outbox rows in v1.
Backend enforcement rule: Dispatcher must lease or claim outbox rows safely avoid duplicate publish where possible and rely on idempotency keys where duplicate publish is possible. It must not inspect or mutate feature domain state beyond job-processing persistence.
Request contract: No HTTP request. Worker config selects queues batch size poll interval and provider adapter.
Response contract: Dispatch summary for logs/metrics including published count skipped count failed count and next poll delay.
Error contract: Provider unavailable publish timeout duplicate provider job id stale outbox lease and persistence failure errors should be recorded safely without losing the durable request.
Cross-feature seams: BullMQ adapter is provider-specific and hidden behind the job-processing provider boundary.
Persistence impact: Updates outbox dispatch state provider job id dispatch attempts lockedBy lockedUntil last error and dispatchedAt.
Indexes / uniqueness: Index on dispatch status runAt priority lockedUntil and createdAt. Provider job id should be unique when present.
Search / filter model: Internal polling by pending dispatch state only in v1.
Compatibility / migration notes: If BullMQ is replaced later the dispatcher/provider adapter boundary should change without forcing feature enqueue callers to change.
Authorization enforcement layer: Worker runtime and repository lease checks.
Audit requirement: Dispatch failures and repeated publish failures should be operationally visible; future operator APIs may expose them.
Privacy / personal data impact: Payload handling should avoid logging sensitive payload bodies. Provider metadata should not contain secrets.
Standards impact: High reliability relevance because this is the bridge between PostgreSQL durable intent and Redis execution.
Acceptance notes: Acceptable when committed outbox rows are eventually published to BullMQ idempotently and failed dispatch remains durable and retryable.

Business goal: Provide an explicit registry of supported job types payload versions handler ownership queue defaults retry policy and execution scope.
User outcome: Feature teams can add async handlers through a governed platform seam instead of ad hoc timers or direct BullMQ imports.
Notes / constraints: Registration should be explicit at platform/worker composition time. Each job type declares owner feature payload schema versions execution scope default queue priority retry policy and handler. No hidden auto-discovery in v1.
Tenant context rule: job type declares root tenant platform-internal or explicitly approved shared-cross-tenant scope
Allowed root roles: RootUserAdmin for future registry inspection if exposed
Explicitly denied roles: unregistered handlers; hidden runtime discovery; direct provider use by features
Authorization summary: Only registered job types can be enqueued or executed. Features may own handlers but the platform registry controls registration and provider binding.
Backend enforcement rule: Worker startup must fail fast or mark configuration invalid when duplicate job types unsupported versions missing schemas or invalid queue defaults are registered.
Request contract: Job type definition includes jobType ownerFeature supportedPayloadVersions schema executionScope defaultQueue defaultPriority retryPolicy concurrency hints timeout hints and handler reference.
Response contract: Registry build returns deterministic registered job-type catalog for worker runtime and validation.
Error contract: Duplicate job type unsupported execution scope missing schema missing handler invalid queue or invalid retry policy errors.
Cross-feature seams: Feature-owned handlers such as notificationDelivery send-email worker may register through their feature integration or worker integration seam.
Persistence impact: No direct persistence unless registry snapshot is later persisted for operator APIs. V1 may persist effective job metadata per job at enqueue time.
Indexes / uniqueness: Not applicable unless a later registry table is added.
Search / filter model: Future operator APIs may read registered job-type metadata.
Compatibility / migration notes: Registry schema should avoid BullMQ-specific public types so provider replacement remains viable.
Authorization enforcement layer: Startup validation plus enqueue and worker execution validation.
Audit requirement: Configuration errors should fail loudly during startup. Future registry changes may be audit-visible if runtime overrides are added.
Privacy / personal data impact: No payload data should be stored in static registry definitions.
Standards impact: High anti-drift relevance because registered job types become shared platform contracts.
Acceptance notes: Acceptable when only explicitly registered job types with versioned schemas and declared scope can be enqueued or executed.

Business goal: Run registered job handlers through BullMQ workers using at-least-once semantics while preserving durable execution status.
User outcome: Background work runs outside HTTP requests with retries crash recovery and auditable attempts.
Notes / constraints: BullMQ owns live queue locks and stalled-job recovery. The platform records enough job and attempt state for audit progress and future operator visibility. Handlers must be idempotent because jobs may run more than once.
Tenant context rule: tenant-scoped handlers must execute within exactly one declared tenant context and verify object ownership through tenant-scoped feature seams
Allowed root roles: RootUserAdmin for future manual controls if exposed
Explicitly denied roles: unauthenticated callers; normal request clients; unregistered job types
Authorization summary: Only internal worker runtime executes jobs. Business authorization is normally checked at enqueue time while execution uses constrained system authority plus current domain-state validation.
Backend enforcement rule: Worker must validate job type payload version payload schema scope and idempotency posture before invoking the handler. It must record attempt start finish status workerId and safe failure summary.
Session / expiry behavior: No session behavior. Original requester session or token must not be replayed.
Request contract: No HTTP request. BullMQ job data contains provider-neutral job id and execution metadata sufficient to load durable job request and validate payload.
Response contract: Execution result updates durable job and attempt state and returns provider-level completion to BullMQ.
Error contract: Unknown job type invalid payload stale/canceled job non-retryable handler error retryable handler error timeout and persistence failure errors.
Cross-feature seams: Handlers may call owning feature services through exported seams only. Features must not import private persistence from other features to complete a job.
Persistence impact: Creates attempt records updates job status and stores safe error summaries and terminal status.
Indexes / uniqueness: Index on job status jobType queueName runAt attemptCount completedAt and worker attempt fields.
Search / filter model: Future operator filters by status queue job type and time are designed for but may be deferred.
Compatibility / migration notes: Execution semantics should remain provider-neutral even though BullMQ is the first engine.
Authorization enforcement layer: Worker runtime validation and feature handler domain validation.
Audit requirement: Attempt lifecycle and terminal failures should be durably visible. Operator-triggered retries later must be audited.
Privacy / personal data impact: Payloads and error summaries must be redacted and must not log secrets tokens credentials or raw provider secrets.
Standards impact: High reliability and security relevance because background jobs run outside request auth context.
Acceptance notes: Acceptable when registered handlers run at least once with durable attempt records safe failure handling and idempotency expectations.

Business goal: Apply consistent retry behavior with exponential backoff jitter max attempts and terminal dead-letter state.
User outcome: Transient failures recover automatically without retry storms and exhausted jobs remain inspectable for future operator action.
Notes / constraints: Default policy should be maxAttempts 5 initialDelay 30 seconds exponential backoff jitter enabled and maxDelay 30 minutes unless a registered job type declares an approved override. Handler errors should be classified retryable or non-retryable.
Tenant context rule: no tenant decision beyond persisted job scope
Allowed root roles: RootUserAdmin for future retry/cancel controls if exposed
Explicitly denied roles: public callers; direct tenant retry controls in v1
Authorization summary: Retry is automatic through the worker runtime in v1. Manual retry is deferred but the model must support future root-operator retry with audit.
Backend enforcement rule: Worker must record every attempt and move exhausted jobs to dead state without deleting history. Non-retryable errors should not churn through all attempts unless policy says otherwise.
Request contract: Retry policy comes from registered job type or constrained enqueue override. No public request in v1.
Response contract: Durable job status and attempt history show retry schedule nextRunAt attempt count and dead-letter reason.
Error contract: Invalid retry policy retryable failure non-retryable failure exhausted attempts and provider scheduling failure.
Cross-feature seams: BullMQ backoff configuration hidden behind provider adapter. Durable status remains platform-owned.
Persistence impact: Updates attempt history nextRunAt status deadLetterReason and terminal timestamps.
Indexes / uniqueness: Index on status nextRunAt jobType and dead-letter status for dispatcher/worker and future operator reads.
Search / filter model: Future operator APIs may filter dead retryable and delayed jobs.
Compatibility / migration notes: Retry model should translate to future SQS or RabbitMQ provider where possible. Platform contract owns semantics not BullMQ specifics.
Audit requirement: Dead-letter and future manual retry/cancel actions must be audit-visible.
Privacy / personal data impact: Error summaries must be safe and redacted.
Acceptance notes: Acceptable when retryable jobs back off with jitter exhausted jobs become dead and history is preserved for future operator retry.

Business goal: Require every job payload to be small versioned JSON validated by the owning registered handler contract.
User outcome: Queued work remains evolvable and safe to replay retry inspect and migrate as handlers change.
Notes / constraints: Payloads should contain stable references and minimal execution metadata by default. Historical snapshots require explicit design exception and durable ownership by the feature. This gate should be added to feature-design and harness planning for job-producing capabilities.
Tenant context rule: tenant payloads must include exactly one tenant id when scope requires it; payload must not infer tenant context from mutable body data
Allowed root roles: RootUserAdmin for future operator inspection if exposed
Explicitly denied roles: unversioned payloads; secret-bearing payloads; broad authority claims
Authorization summary: Feature enqueue callers must pass a supported payload version and schema-valid JSON before the job request is accepted.
Backend enforcement rule: Enqueue and worker execution both validate payload version and schema. Unsafe fields and oversized payloads should be rejected or redacted according to policy.
Session / expiry behavior: No session behavior. Payload must not include sessions bearer tokens or live permission claims.
Request contract: Input is jobType payloadVersion and JSON payload. Payload size limit and forbidden-field patterns should be declared in platform policy.
Response contract: Returns validated normalized payload metadata or validation failure.
Error contract: Unsupported version invalid schema oversized payload forbidden secret/token field missing stable reference and unsafe snapshot exception errors.
Cross-feature seams: Owning feature supplies schemas for its job types. The foundation enforces common safety rules.
Persistence impact: May persist payload JSON and safe metadata. Operator display should later use redacted metadata not raw payload by default.
Indexes / uniqueness: Indexes should not depend on arbitrary payload JSON. Persist important searchable fields as explicit metadata when needed.
Search / filter model: No generic JSON search in v1.
Compatibility / migration notes: Payload versioning allows handler evolution without breaking queued historical jobs.
Authorization enforcement layer: Registry schema validation and common payload safety checks.
Audit requirement: Unsafe payload rejection should be visible in tests and logs. Future operator APIs must not expose full sensitive payloads.
Privacy / personal data impact: Potentially high privacy impact; payloads must avoid personal data unless necessary and must never carry secrets credentials tokens or authority grants.
Standards impact: High security and anti-drift relevance. This is a feature-design gate for all job-backed features.
Acceptance notes: Acceptable when unversioned oversized secret-bearing or authority-bearing payloads are rejected and job-producing feature plans classify any snapshot exceptions.

Business goal: Ensure every job type declares whether it is root tenant platform-internal or explicitly approved shared-cross-tenant work.
User outcome: Async execution cannot bypass tenant isolation or replay stale request authority.
Notes / constraints: Jobs should carry stable context such as tenantId entity IDs and requester audit IDs but must not carry bearer tokens sessions role claims permission lists or credentials. Tenant-scoped handlers must load domain objects through tenant-scoped seams and verify ownership.
Primary actor: feature-owned backend service and platform worker
Tenant context rule: tenant-scoped jobs require exactly one tenant context per job; shared-cross-tenant jobs require explicit approval and design documentation
Explicitly denied roles: implicit cross-tenant jobs; tenant context from mutable payload bodies; token replay
Authorization summary: Authorization is normally checked at enqueue time by the feature capability. Execution runs under constrained system authority with scope and current domain-state validation.
Backend enforcement rule: Registry validation must require execution scope. Tenant handlers must verify object ownership through tenant-scoped repository/service calls. Cross-tenant jobs must be blocked unless explicitly approved.
Session / expiry behavior: No session replay. Requester identity is audit attribution only.
Route(s): Internal validation and handler execution only
Request contract: Job type definition declares execution scope. Enqueue request includes tenantId when required and requester audit attribution when available.
Response contract: Returns persisted scope metadata and rejects missing or invalid scope context.
Error contract: Missing tenant context ambiguous tenant context unauthorized shared-cross-tenant scope token-bearing payload and object-tenant mismatch errors.
Cross-feature seams: Feature handlers consume owning feature seams and may call approved public seams only.
Persistence impact: Persists execution scope tenantId when required and requester audit attribution. Avoids using mutable related records as the only durable scope fact.
Indexes / uniqueness: Index on executionScope tenantId jobType and related domain metadata if future operator filters need it.
Search / filter model: Future operator filters by scope and tenant should use explicit scalar columns not JSON payload search.
Compatibility / migration notes: This rule preserves repo tenant-boundary defaults as async work grows.
Authorization enforcement layer: Registry validation enqueue validation and handler domain checks.
Audit requirement: Scope violations and future operator cross-tenant actions should be audit-visible.
Privacy / personal data impact: Tenant ids actor ids and entity ids are sensitive operational metadata and should be least-privilege in future APIs.
Standards impact: Very high security relevance because jobs run outside request authz middleware.
Acceptance notes: Acceptable when jobs cannot smuggle authority and tenant-scoped handlers prove object ownership in exactly one tenant context.

Business goal: Define queue assignment priority bands and worker concurrency defaults so slow or bulk workloads do not block routine or critical jobs.
User outcome: Routine security and transactional work remains responsive even when bulk jobs fan out into large workloads.
Notes / constraints: Initial queues should be critical default bulk and maintenance. Priority bands should be numeric but separate queues and chunking are the main isolation tools. Initial implementation supports queue-level concurrency and job-type defaults while preserving room for runtime overrides later.
Tenant context rule: no tenant-specific rule; queue selection follows job type and operational profile
Explicitly denied roles: public callers; tenant actors setting queue priority directly
Authorization summary: Feature code may request allowed defaults but cannot arbitrarily boost work into critical queues without registered policy.
Frontend visibility rule: No frontend surface in v1. Future operator UI may show queues and overrides.
Backend enforcement rule: Registry must constrain queue and priority values. Worker runtime must honor queue-level concurrency. Long-running work should be chunked instead of monopolizing workers.
Request contract: Job type definition declares defaultQueue defaultPriority concurrency hint and optional rate-limit hint. Runtime config supplies queue-level worker concurrency.
Response contract: Effective worker configuration and job metadata reflect queue priority and concurrency defaults.
Error contract: Invalid queue unknown priority band unauthorized critical queue selection and invalid concurrency configuration errors.
Cross-feature seams: BullMQ queues are provider-specific implementation behind platform queue names.
Persistence impact: Persists effective queueName priority and possibly concurrency snapshot per job. Runtime config may not require persistence in v1.
Indexes / uniqueness: Index on queueName priority runAt status and createdAt to support dispatch ordering and future operator reads.
Search / filter model: Future operator APIs may filter queue and priority metadata.
Compatibility / migration notes: Runtime overrides for queue priority concurrency pause resume and rate limits are deferred but should fit the model later.
Authorization enforcement layer: Registry validation and worker runtime configuration.
Audit requirement: Future operator changes to queue config must be audited.
Privacy / personal data impact: Low privacy impact unless queue metadata reveals sensitive workflow names.
Standards impact: Operational reliability relevance because workload isolation prevents bulk starvation of routine tasks.
Acceptance notes: Acceptable when critical default bulk and maintenance queues have configurable worker concurrency and job-type defaults prevent bulk work from blocking routine work.

Business goal: Persist job and attempt metadata needed for later root-operator inspection retry cancel queue health and worker health APIs without exposing those APIs in the first slice.
User outcome: If trouble appears later operators can pick up from durable history instead of reverse-engineering Redis state.
Notes / constraints: Operator APIs and UI are deferred but the schema must preserve job id queue name job type payload version redacted payload metadata status priority runAt attempt count max attempts timestamps worker id error summary related domain references idempotency key dead-letter state and future audit trail hooks.
Tenant context rule: tenant metadata should be stored only in explicit scope fields and protected by future root/operator access
Authorization summary: No operator read API exists in v1. Future APIs should be root-authorized and audited.
Frontend visibility rule: No frontend in v1. Future root-admin Operations Jobs page may consume this metadata.
Backend enforcement rule: Persistence writes must store safe metadata. Full payload display must be redacted by default and secrets must never be persisted or exposed.
Session / expiry behavior: Future APIs use root session semantics.
Client-side permission behavior: Future UI must hide job operations without governing capabilities.
Route(s): Future candidates: GET /v1/job-processing/jobs GET /v1/job-processing/jobs/:jobId GET /v1/job-processing/queues GET /v1/job-processing/workers
Request contract: Deferred. Future queries filter by queue jobType status tenantId related entity dead-letter state and time range.
Response contract: Deferred. Future responses expose safe metadata attempts and redacted payload display only.
Error contract: Future errors include validation authz not-found stale status and unsafe disclosure protections.
Cross-feature seams: Feature-owned progress APIs remain separate from generic job APIs.
Persistence impact: Creates durable job and attempt metadata designed for future operator read retry cancel and queue health surfaces.
Indexes / uniqueness: Index on status queueName jobType tenantId relatedEntityType relatedEntityId createdAt updatedAt completedAt and deadLetter state.
Search / filter model: Future operator search should use explicit scalar columns not raw payload search.
Session / auth dependency: Future root session for APIs. No v1 session dependency.
Compatibility / migration notes: Deferred APIs should not require redesigning execution semantics.
Authentication requirement: No v1 external auth. Future root auth required.
Authorization enforcement layer: Future root authz capability enforcement plus feature-level redaction guards.
CSP / browser security impact: No browser impact until UI is added.
Audit requirement: Future successful and denied read/retry/cancel actions should be audited. V1 stores enough attribution to support that trail later.
Privacy / personal data impact: Moderate to high; metadata may include tenant and entity references and error summaries. Redaction is required.
Acceptance notes: Acceptable when v1 can run without operator APIs while preserving enough durable metadata to add honest troubleshooting controls later.

Business goal: Preserve model support for future root-operator manual retry cancel and queue management without making those APIs part of the first implementation.
User outcome: The team can add safe operator controls later when real operational failures justify them.
Notes / constraints: Manual retry cancel pause resume and queue management are deferred. The data model should distinguish retryable failed dead canceled running delayed and succeeded states and preserve prior attempts so manual actions do not erase history.
Tenant context rule: no tenant operator action in v1; future root operator actions over tenant-scoped jobs require audit and least-privilege controls
Explicitly denied roles: tenant actors; unauthenticated callers; root users without future job-processing capabilities
Authorization summary: Future manual controls require explicit root authz capabilities and audit. No manual controls are exposed in v1.
Frontend visibility rule: Future UI should show controls only when allowed and only for states where the operation is safe.
Backend enforcement rule: V1 state machine must not collapse terminal statuses in a way that prevents future retry/cancel semantics. Future mutation APIs must validate state transitions and idempotency.
Route(s): Future candidates: POST /v1/job-processing/jobs/:jobId/retry POST /v1/job-processing/jobs/:jobId/cancel POST /v1/job-processing/queues/:queueName/pause POST /v1/job-processing/queues/:queueName/resume
Request contract: Future requests include reason state precondition optional filters and possibly max batch size.
Response contract: Future responses include updated job/queue state audit id and retry/cancel result summary.
Error contract: Future errors include invalid state stale precondition unauthorized unsafe retry non-idempotent handler and partial batch failure.
Cross-feature seams: Feature-owned domain state may need coordinated cancel/retry hooks before generic controls operate on some job types.
Persistence impact: V1 stores statuses and attempts in a way that can support future manual transitions without deleting history.
Indexes / uniqueness: Indexes for future terminal-state and dead-letter queries should be present from v1 where cheap.
Search / filter model: Future filter model explicit by status job type queue and related entity.
Compatibility / migration notes: Manual actions should be added only after ADR/PRD update if semantics become cross-cutting.
Authorization enforcement layer: Future root authz plus state-transition validation.
Audit requirement: Future retry cancel pause resume actions must be audited with actor reason and affected jobs.
Privacy / personal data impact: Moderate privacy and security risk because operator controls can re-run tenant-affecting work.
Acceptance notes: Acceptable when v1 deliberately defers controls but terminal statuses attempt history and audit hooks make future controls feasible.

Business goal: Define how batch features should use durable item-level domain state for interruption recovery progress UI and ETA rather than relying on queue memory.
User outcome: Large asynchronous workflows can resume after crashes and later expose accurate business progress.
Notes / constraints: The queue foundation tracks generic job state. User-facing progress should usually come from feature-owned domain item records such as campaign recipients import rows or export chunks. Batch jobs should fan out into small idempotent chunk jobs and persist item statuses.
Capability boundary (root - tenant - sha: tenant or root depending on owning feature
Tenant context rule: batch item state must follow the owning feature scope and tenant boundary
Allowed root roles: RootUserAdmin where root-owned batch work applies
Explicitly denied roles: unauthenticated callers; cross-tenant batch operations without explicit approval
Authorization summary: Owning feature authorizes batch creation. Job foundation provides guidance and generic execution but does not own business progress semantics.
Frontend visibility rule: Future feature UI may show progress through feature-owned APIs not generic job APIs.
Backend enforcement rule: Feature handlers should claim chunks durably and mark item-level states such as pending queued processing succeeded failed dead or canceled. Long-running work should be split into chunks.
Frontend required?: No per foundation; yes in consuming features
Request contract: Feature-owned APIs should expose total pending queued running succeeded failed dead canceled recent throughput and approximate ETA where useful.
Response contract: Feature-owned progress responses should be domain meaningful such as campaign recipients sent or import rows processed not just raw job counts.
Feature seam(s): jobProcessing batch guidance and enqueue seam
Cross-feature seams: Consuming features such as campaign email imports exports and reconciliation jobs own item records and progress APIs.
Persistence impact: No generic batch-item table in v1. Consuming features persist their own item-level progress where needed.
Migration required?: No for foundation; yes for consuming batch features
Indexes / uniqueness: Consuming features need indexes on batch id status claimedUntil timestamps and item identity.
Search / filter model: Generic job payload search is not a substitute for domain progress queries.
Compatibility / migration notes: This is a design gate not a generic batch engine in v1.
Authorization enforcement layer: Owning feature authz plus job scope checks.
Audit requirement: Batch progress and manual retries should be audit-visible in owning feature when business-sensitive.
Privacy / personal data impact: Potentially high depending on domain item data. Queue payload should carry ids not full item data.
Frontend tests: Future feature UI tests when progress UI exists
Acceptance notes: Acceptable when batch-capable features model per-item durable progress and interrupted workers can resume from database state.

Business goal: Ensure worker processes have stable identity and can stop accepting new work while preserving or completing in-flight jobs during deploys and restarts.
User outcome: Deploys and crashes do not create ambiguous job history or unnecessary duplicate work.
Notes / constraints: Worker identity should include process host pid or generated boot id. Worker shutdown should handle SIGTERM and SIGINT stop accepting new jobs close BullMQ workers and allow a bounded in-flight drain timeout.
Allowed root roles: RootUserAdmin for future worker health APIs
Authorization summary: Only platform worker runtime owns worker lifecycle.
Frontend visibility rule: No frontend in v1. Future worker-health UI may display worker identity and heartbeats.
Backend enforcement rule: Worker runtime must record worker id on attempts and shut down cleanly when signaled. Long jobs should be chunked rather than relying on very long locks.
Request contract: Runtime config includes workerId drain timeout queue list and concurrency.
Response contract: Logs and future metadata show worker identity attempt ownership and shutdown outcome.
Error contract: Shutdown timeout provider close failure stalled job and persistence failure errors.
Cross-feature seams: BullMQ lock and stalled-job mechanics are hidden behind provider adapter while durable attempt records store worker identity.
Persistence impact: Attempt records store workerId startedAt finishedAt and status. Future worker heartbeat table may be added later if operator health APIs need it.
Migration required?: Maybe if worker heartbeat persistence is included later
Indexes / uniqueness: Index on attempt workerId and timestamps if worker troubleshooting is needed.
Search / filter model: Future operator worker filters by worker id and time.
Compatibility / migration notes: Provider replacement should preserve worker identity semantics even if lock mechanics differ.
Authorization enforcement layer: Signal handling and runtime lifecycle management.
Audit requirement: Worker lifecycle events may be logged and future health events may be auditable if operationally significant.
Acceptance notes: Acceptable when workers record stable identity and handle graceful shutdown without losing durable job state.

Business goal: Keep the first slice compatible with delayed jobs while deferring a full recurring scheduling toolkit to a later platform layer.
User outcome: The platform can run immediate and simple delayed work now without prematurely designing cron and calendar workflows.
Notes / constraints: V1 should support runAt/delayed execution because retry backoff and scheduled dispatch need it. Recurring jobs cron scheduling calendars and schedule-management UI are deferred.
Explicitly denied roles: public schedule mutation; hidden recurring jobs without design approval
Authorization summary: Only internal job-processing and registered features may use simple runAt. Recurring schedules require a later approved capability matrix/PRD.
Frontend visibility rule: No frontend in v1. Future scheduling UI deferred.
Backend enforcement rule: Enqueue validation accepts optional runAt for delayed jobs. No recurring schedule definitions are persisted in v1 unless a later slice adds them.
Request contract: Optional runAt timestamp on enqueue. No cron expression contract in v1.
Response contract: Job metadata shows runAt and delayed status.
Error contract: Invalid runAt past/future bounds unsupported recurring schedule and provider delay error.
Cross-feature seams: Future scheduling toolkit should build on enqueue seam without requiring feature handlers to change.
Persistence impact: Stores runAt and status. No schedule table in v1.
Indexes / uniqueness: Index on runAt status queueName priority.
Search / filter model: Future filters by delayed status and runAt.
Compatibility / migration notes: Do not let simple delayed jobs be mistaken for approved recurring scheduling toolkit.
Authorization enforcement layer: Enqueue validation and dispatcher/worker delay handling.
Audit requirement: Future schedule management must be audited. V1 delayed enqueue audit depends on owning feature.
Privacy / personal data impact: Low to moderate depending on payload metadata.
Standards impact: Architecture relevance because scheduling is intentionally deferred.
Acceptance notes: Acceptable when delayed one-off jobs work but recurring scheduling remains explicitly deferred.

Business goal: Preserve a clear first-consumer path for notificationDelivery automatic retry without forcing that adoption into the foundation planning slice.
User outcome: Email delivery can later use the queue foundation for automatic retry through existing logical email and attempt records.
Notes / constraints: notificationDelivery already has durable outbound email and attempt history and notes automatic background retry as future work. This planning slice should align the job foundation so a later notificationDelivery adoption can enqueue notification.email.send jobs carrying outboundEmailId.
Capability boundary (root - tenant - sha: shared or platform-internal depending on notification context
Tenant context rule: tenant metadata may be attached but notificationDelivery should not infer broad tenant authority from the job payload
Explicitly denied roles: unauthenticated callers; direct public email send jobs
Authorization summary: Future adoption should call jobProcessing from notificationDelivery or caller workflows through approved seams. First planning slice does not change notificationDelivery behavior.
Backend enforcement rule: Later handler must load outboundEmailId from notificationDelivery durable records and create attempts idempotently. Payload should not carry raw email body unless a durable snapshot exception is approved.
Frontend route: Future notificationDelivery APIs unchanged unless operator retry APIs added later
Frontend states: Root session for operator routes where applicable
Route(s): Future internal worker handler not public route
Request contract: Payload likely includes outboundEmailId only plus optional requested attempt context.
Response contract: Returns generic job status through jobProcessing and delivery status through notificationDelivery domain records.
Error contract: Delivery provider errors retryable or non-retryable unsafe resend duplicate send and missing outboundEmail errors.
Cross-feature seams: Consumes notificationDelivery public seam and jobProcessing enqueue/execution seam.
Persistence impact: No change in this planning slice. Later adoption may add job-processing records and perhaps adjust outbound email attempt timing.
Indexes / uniqueness: Indexes already exist for notification attempts; jobProcessing indexes cover job state.
Search / filter model: Future operator and notificationDelivery filters remain distinct.
Session / auth dependency: Existing root session for operator email routes only.
Compatibility / migration notes: Adoption should be a separate loop with test cases and docs updates.
Authentication requirement: Existing auth requirements plus job-processing internal execution.
Authorization enforcement layer: Existing route authz plus worker validation.
Audit requirement: Email send attempts and future retries must remain audit-visible.
Privacy / personal data impact: High because email metadata and content snapshots may be personal or sensitive.
Standards impact: High because this is the likely first real consumer of the queue foundation.
Acceptance notes: Acceptable when the planning artifacts leave a clean adoption path for automatic email retry without mixing it into the first foundation implementation.
